title: How Friday closed
text: Friday ended in the red for most of our list. The S&P 500 fund SPY slipped 0.4% and the Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ fell 1.2%, led by chip stocks. Two things weighed on the market: a hot report on wholesale prices, and traders selling chip stocks that had jumped earlier in the week. Even so, news reports say the Nasdaq still had its best week since August. A few steady names went up: Eli Lilly, Meta, Microsoft and the dividend fund SCHD.

title: AMD had the biggest drop on our list
text: AMD fell 8.8% to $534.06. Earlier this week many traders bought AMD and Broadcom, guessing they would win business if NVIDIA struggled after its CEO left. On Friday a lot of them sold to lock in gains, and Broadcom fell 4.8% too. AMD is still 73% of the way up its one year range, so it has not lost most of its recent climb. Our risk score for AMD went up a little, from 7.3 to 7.5, which is in the high zone.

title: Wholesale prices are rising fast
text: The producer price index, which tracks prices businesses pay each other, rose 0.3% in October. That was a bit less than experts expected for the month. But compared with a year ago, prices were up 6.5%, the fastest pace since November 2022. Fast rising prices can push the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates. Traders are now betting on a rate hike in December, and the 10 year Treasury yield is sitting above 5%.

title: NVIDIA is close to its one year low
text: NVIDIA fell 2.0% to $162.85. It is now only 15% of the way up its one year range. Its lowest price of the past year was $148.80, so it is about 9% above that level. Analysts' average target is $321, almost double today's price, but targets are guesses and can be cut. NVIDIA's risk score stays at 6.0, in the medium zone.

title: Steady names held up
text: Not everything went down. Eli Lilly rose 1.4% to $1,445.40, very close to its one year high of $1,460. The dividend fund SCHD rose 0.5% and is also near its high. Meta rose 2.9%. On a day when fast growing chip stocks fall, companies with steadier sales sometimes hold up better. That is one reason people spread money across different kinds of companies.

title: Lesson 51: What is profit-taking?
text: Profit-taking means selling a stock after its price went up, to lock in the gain. Imagine you buy a trading card for $10, and a week later everyone wants it and it is worth $15. If you sell it, you take your $5 profit. When a stock jumps fast, like AMD did earlier this week, many people take profits at the same time. All that selling can push the price down, even if nothing bad happened at the company. So a drop after a big jump does not always mean the company is in trouble. It can just mean people are cashing in.
